0. Warm-up — What counts as a precise instruction?
Imagine you are giving instructions to a computer.
Which instruction is more executable?
A. “Calculate the total sales.”
B. “Add Monday, Tuesday, and Wednesday sales and store the result as total_sales.”

Your task
Write one reason why B is more suitable for a computer.
Your answer:
…

title: DSA105 — Fundamentals of Algorithms and Programming
text:
1. Today’s Domain Problem
A small store records sales for three days:

Monday: 1,250 TL
Tuesday: 1,480 TL
Wednesday: 1,320 TL

We want to calculate:

the total sales;
the average daily sales.

Before touching Python, identify the computational structure.

ACTIVITY 1 — Input → Process → Output
Complete the table in your own notes.



Element
What belongs here?




Input
?


Process
?


Output
?



Pair check (2 minutes): Compare your answers with the person next to you.

title: DSA105 — Fundamentals of Algorithms and Programming
text:
2. Algorithm = A Precise Sequence
An algorithm is a finite and unambiguous sequence of steps for solving a problem.
A useful beginner checklist:

Input: What information enters the solution?
Process: What operations transform the information?
Output: What result must be produced?
Order: In which sequence must the steps happen?
Termination: Does the procedure end?


ACTIVITY 2 — Put the algorithm in order
The following steps are mixed.
A. Display the total and average.
B. Read the three daily sales values.
C. Start.
D. Calculate the average as total / 3.
E. Calculate the total of the three sales values.
F. End.
Write the correct order:
___ → ___ → ___ → ___ → ___ → ___


ACTIVITY 3 — Find the ambiguity
Consider this instruction:

“Take the sales numbers, do the necessary calculation, and show the result.”

Identify two things that are unclear.

…
…

title: DSA105 — Fundamentals of Algorithms and Programming
section: 3. First Executable Object — Do not worry about Python grammar yet
text:
3. First Executable Object — Do not worry about Python grammar yet
The code below is simply an executable representation of the algorithm.

PREDICT BEFORE YOU RUN
What values do you expect for total_sales and average_sales?

monday_sales = 1250
tuesday_sales = 1480
wednesday_sales = 1320

total_sales = monday_sales + tuesday_sales + wednesday_sales
average_sales = total_sales / 3

print("Total sales:", total_sales)
print("Average daily sales:", average_sales)



ACTIVITY 4 — Run and compare

Run the cell.
Compare the result with your prediction.
If your prediction was wrong, identify which step in your reasoning was wrong.

One-sentence explanation:
…


ACTIVITY 5 — Modify
Change the data:

Monday: 900
Tuesday: 1,100
Wednesday: 1,300

Before running the code, predict the new total and average.
Then modify the code cell below and test your prediction.

monday_sales = 900
tuesday_sales = 1100
wednesday_sales = 1300

# Complete these two lines:
total_sales = ...
average_sales = ...

print("Total sales:", total_sales)
print("Average daily sales:", average_sales)

title: DSA105 — Fundamentals of Algorithms and Programming
text:
4. From Algorithm to Flowchart
For Week 1 we will use four basic flowchart elements:

Start / End
Input / Output
Process
Arrow / flow direction

We will introduce decision symbols later when we study conditional logic.
The store-sales algorithm can be represented as:
Start → Read sales → Calculate total → Calculate average → Display results → End

ACTIVITY 6 — Match the step to the flowchart role
For each step, decide whether it is Start/End, Input/Output, or Process.

Read Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday sales → ______
Calculate total_sales → ______
Display average_sales → ______
End → ______

title: DSA105 — Fundamentals of Algorithms and Programming
text:
5. Human CPU Challenge
Work in pairs.

Student A — Programmer
Write an algorithm for this task:

A shop knows the unit price and quantity sold. Calculate total revenue.



Student B — Computer
Follow the instructions literally. Do not repair unclear instructions.
Then switch roles.


Debrief
What kind of instruction caused the most confusion?

title: DSA105 — Fundamentals of Algorithms and Programming
text:
6. Faded Example — Complete, Don’t Copy
A café sold 42 coffees at 75 TL each.
Complete the missing parts.

unit_price = 75
quantity = 42

revenue = ____________________

print("Revenue:", ____________________)


ACTIVITY 7 — Explain
Without using the words “because Python says so,” explain:

Why must revenue be calculated after unit_price and quantity are known?

Your answer:
…

title: DSA105 — Fundamentals of Algorithms and Programming
section: 7. Debug the Algorithm, Not the Syntax
text:
7. Debug the Algorithm, Not the Syntax
A student wrote:

Display total revenue.
Read unit price.
End.
Read quantity.
Calculate revenue = unit price × quantity.
Start.


Your task
Rewrite the algorithm in a valid order.
Then answer:

Is this a syntax problem or an algorithmic sequencing problem?

title: DSA105 — Fundamentals of Algorithms and Programming
text:
8. Independent Build — Lab Evidence Task

Scenario
A company sold three products today:

Product A revenue: 2,400 TL
Product B revenue: 3,150 TL
Product C revenue: 1,950 TL



Your job

Identify Input → Process → Output.
Write a 5–7 step algorithm.
Implement the total revenue calculation in Python.
Predict the output before running.
Run and verify.

Use the cell below.

# Write your implementation here

product_a = 2400
product_b = 3150
product_c = 1950

# TODO: calculate total revenue



LAB EVIDENCE
Submit the requested Week 1 lab evidence through the class Google Form.
You will submit: - your predicted output; - your actual output; - one sentence explaining whether they matched; - your algorithm in 5–7 steps.
Instructor will provide the form link.

title: DSA105 — Fundamentals of Algorithms and Programming
text:
9. Exit Reflection
Before leaving class, be ready to answer:

What is the difference between an algorithm and a program?
Which part was most difficult today: defining input, defining process, defining output, ordering steps, or reading code?
Confidence (1–5): “I can convert a simple problem into an ordered algorithm.”

Submit these in the Week 1 Exit Ticket Form.

text:

You will receive a separate Week 1 homework notebook.
The goal is not to write complex Python.
The goal is to show that you can move through:
Problem → IPO → Algorithm → Executable representation → Verification

title: Course Guide
text:
The learning model
DSA105 treats programming as a way of making reasoning explicit, executable, and testable.
The recurring classroom cycle is:

Do → Observe → Name → Explain → Do Again

You will rarely remain passive for long periods. Most class segments require a visible action: predict an output, modify code, explain a result, complete a partial implementation, debug a mistake, or build a small solution.

title: Course Guide
text:
Why Python?
Python is used because it turns abstract ideas into concrete outcomes that can be executed immediately.
The relationship is:
Computational idea → Algorithm → Python representation → Output → Verification
Python is therefore both: - a programming language that you must learn to use; and - a concrete surface on which computational reasoning can be tested.

title: Course Guide
text:
Class timing: 14:20–16:40
DSA105 is scheduled as three 40-minute class hours. This gives 120 minutes of effective teaching time within the 14:20–16:40 block.
For TRACE Studio, the block is organized as two longer active-learning sessions:









Clock time
Duration
Phase
Typical student activity




14:20–15:20
60 min
Session 1
retrieval, problem framing, prediction, micro-lecture, guided coding


15:20–15:35
15 min
Break
—


15:35–16:35
60 min
Session 2
guided lab, pair challenge, debugging, domain application, evidence task


16:35–16:40
5 min
Close / transition
exit instruction, submission check, next-step reminder



The two 60-minute sessions preserve the full 120 minutes of instructional activity while reducing fragmentation. The final five minutes are treated as a transition buffer rather than additional teaching time.

Internal rhythm of each 60-minute session
A 60-minute session should still avoid long passive stretches. A typical internal rhythm is:

10–15 min: problem / prediction / retrieval;
10–15 min: focused explanation or live coding;
15–20 min: guided student action;
10–15 min: pair task, debugging, explanation, or evidence capture.

The exact distribution can change by week, but students should normally be required to do something observable at least every 10–15 minutes.


Alternative view: official 40-minute class hours
The same 14:20–16:40 block can also be understood as:

14:20–15:00 — Class hour 1
15:00–15:10 — Break
15:10–15:50 — Class hour 2
15:50–16:00 — Break
16:00–16:40 — Class hour 3

TRACE Studio uses the 60 + 15 + 60 delivery pattern operationally, while remaining equivalent to the same 120 minutes of effective teaching time.

text:
Why verification matters
A program can run and still be logically wrong.
An AI-generated solution can be syntactically correct and still misunderstand the problem.
Your responsibility is therefore not only to obtain code, but to understand and test the computational behaviour.

title: DSA105 · TRACE Studio
text:
Official course objective
The course aims to develop basic computer-based problem-solving skills by focusing on algorithm development, flowcharting, and programming logic. Python is used as the primary implementation language. Students work with data types, control structures, functions, and file operations, with examples connected to economics, business, and data analysis. Through hands-on exercises, students practice designing, implementing, testing, and debugging programs while building a foundation for advanced data structures and algorithmic thinking.

title: DSA105 · TRACE Studio
text:
Learning outcomes
By the end of DSA105, you should be able to:

Define computational problems.
Design algorithms for problem solving.
Translate algorithms into Python code.
Test and debug programs effectively.
Integrate programming with economics and business analytics contexts.







NoteWhat this course is not



This is not a course in memorizing Python commands. Python gives us a visible and executable way to test whether our reasoning is precise enough for a computer.

title: DSA105 · TRACE Studio
text:
How the course works


1. Concept
A problem, computational pattern, or domain scenario is introduced.


2. Action
You predict, trace, modify, complete, or build something in Colab.


3. Evidence
A short quiz, lab task, exit ticket, or homework records what you can do.


4. Feedback
Your evidence is combined into a learning portfolio after the midterm.
